title: The Rock Cycle
seo_title: Year 8 Science: The Rock Cycle Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Investigate the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks and describe how they change in the rock cycle over different timescales (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 8 science worksheets on the rock cycle: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, crystal size, fossils, and Australian rocks such as Uluru, Kata Tjuta and the Organ Pipes. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Rocks change from one type to another.
key_sub: Cooling makes igneous rock, layering makes sedimentary rock, heat and pressure make metamorphic rock.
body_html:
How to think about it

Rocks form in three main ways and change from one type to another in the rock cycle.

  • Igneous: magma or lava cools. Slow cooling underground gives large crystals (granite); fast cooling gives small crystals (basalt).
  • Sedimentary: sediments are deposited, compacted and cemented (sandstone, limestone); may contain fossils.
  • Metamorphic: heat and pressure change rock without melting it (marble, slate). Any rock can be weathered, melted or changed again.
Example

Large crystals. Cooled fast or slow?

crystals had time to grow

Answer: slowly

Example

Limestone heated and squeezed becomes…

metamorphism without melting

Answer: marble

Common mistakes

  • Thinking large crystals mean fast cooling.
  • Thinking metamorphic rocks form by melting.
  • Thinking the rock cycle always follows one fixed order.

faq.q: What are the three types of rock?
faq.a: Igneous rocks form from cooled magma or lava, sedimentary rocks from layers of sediment, and metamorphic rocks from rocks changed by heat and pressure.
Uluru is made of arkose, a coarse sandstone. Iron minerals in the rock have rusted, giving it its red colour.

faq.q: Why are fossils found in sedimentary rocks?
faq.a: Sediments bury dead plants and animals gently, so their shapes are preserved. Melting and high pressure would destroy fossils in other rocks.

items.q: Is pumice an igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock?
items.e: Igneous rock is formed when hot, melted rock cools and hardens.

items.q: Is chalk an igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock?
items.e: Sedimentary rock is formed from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together.

items.q: What type of rock is schist?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: What type of rock is marble?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
c: Weathering breaks rock down where it is; erosion carries the pieces away.
items.e: Then deposition.

items.q: Which rock forms when limestone is heated and squeezed?
items.e: Limestone is metamorphosed into marble.

items.q: Where are fossils most often found?
items.e: Heat destroys them.

items.q: What type of rock is obsidian?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: What is magma?
items.e: Lava when it erupts.

items.q: Australian opals form in which kind of rock?

items.q: Which of these is a sedimentary rock: basalt, granite, sandstone or slate?

items.q: What type of rock is sandstone?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: What type of rock is mudstone?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: Is marble an igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock?
items.e: Metamorphic rock is formed when other rocks are changed by great heat and pressure.

items.q: Why does granite have large crystals but basalt has small ones?
c: Granite cooled slowly underground; basalt cooled quickly at the surface.
Crystals grow faster at the surface.
items.e: Slow cooling gives time for large crystals to grow.

items.q: How do igneous rocks form?
c: when magma or lava cools and becomes solid
when rocks are heated and squeezed without melting
when layers of sediment are pressed together
items.e: Granite and basalt are igneous.

items.q: Which of these is a sedimentary rock: granite, mudstone, pumice or slate?
items.e: Sedimentary rock is formed from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together.

items.q: How do metamorphic rocks form?
c: existing rocks are changed by heat and pressure without melting
items.e: Marble and slate are metamorphic.

items.q: In which kind of rock are fossils usually found?
items.e: Sediments bury dead organisms gently.

items.q: How do metamorphic rocks form?
c: Existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting.
items.e: Marble, slate.

items.q: Which process turns loose sand into sandstone?
items.e: Minerals in water glue the grains together.

items.q: William asks what energy source drives volcanic eruptions in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
c: the sun (which drives the water cycle)
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Oliver asks what energy source drives melting rock into magma in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
c: the sun (which drives the water cycle)
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Ruby's model shows igneous rock changing into sedimentary rock. Which process causes this?
c: weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation
items.e: In the rock cycle, igneous rock becomes sedimentary rock by weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation.

items.q: William's model shows sedimentary rock changing into igneous rock. Which process causes this?
c: weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation
items.e: In the rock cycle, sedimentary rock becomes igneous rock by melting into magma, then cooling.

items.q: Which energy drives weathering and erosion?
items.e: The sun drives wind and the water cycle.

items.q: Which energy drives melting and metamorphism?
items.e: Deep underground it is very hot.

items.q: What is the difference between magma and lava?
c: Magma is melted rock underground; lava is melted rock on the surface.
items.e: Both cool to form igneous rock.

items.q: Which rock type often contains fossils?
items.e: Layers of sediment can bury organisms.

items.q: Which rock type belongs in the box with the question mark in Zara's diagram?

c: weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation
items.e: In the rock cycle, sedimentary rock becomes metamorphic rock by heat and pressure deep underground.

items.q: What are the three main types of rock?
items.e: They form in different ways.

items.q: Noah asks what energy source drives weathering by rain and ice in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
c: the sun (which drives the water cycle)
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Amelia asks what energy source drives erosion by wind in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Which rock type belongs in the box with the question mark in Isla's diagram?
items.e: Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens.

items.q: Isla's model shows metamorphic rock changing into igneous rock. Which process causes this?
items.e: In the rock cycle, metamorphic rock becomes igneous rock by melting into magma, then cooling.

items.q: Zara's model shows metamorphic rock changing into sedimentary rock. Which process causes this?
c: weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation
items.e: In the rock cycle, metamorphic rock becomes sedimentary rock by weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation.

items.q: Does a rock have to melt to become metamorphic?
c: No. Heat and pressure change it without melting it.
items.e: If it melts, it becomes magma.

items.q: Plant roots grow into cracks and split the rock. What kind of weathering is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock where it is; erosion carries it away.

items.q: What kind of rock is Sydney's harbour cliffs made of?
items.e: It formed from layers of river sand pressed together.

items.q: Ethan finds a rock that forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens. What type of rock is it?
items.e: Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens.

items.q: A river carries pebbles from a mountain to a lake. Which part of the rock cycle is this?

items.q: Jack soaks four rocks of the same size in water and weighs them before and after. Which result shows the most porous rock?
c: the rock with the biggest increase in mass

items.q: A geologist finds a rock with bands of crystals and no fossils. Which type is it most likely to be?
items.e: Banding forms under pressure.

items.q: Why are pebbles on a beach rounded?

items.e: Erosion.

items.q: Which rock fizzes when a drop of acid is put on it?
items.e: Carbonates release carbon dioxide.

items.q: Ruby drops dilute acid on a rock and it fizzes. What does this suggest?
c: The rock contains calcium carbonate, such as limestone or marble.
items.e: Carbonates react with acid to make carbon dioxide.

c: They took millions of years to form and are being used much faster.

items.e: Heavier particles settle first.
